title: Fill in the Blanks and Cloze Tests
shortDescription: The solving skill for gap-filling questions — reading for clues before options, and why cloze passages need a first read-through with no guessing.
genZNote: The blank is not a mystery, it's a puzzle with clues hidden in plain sight. Read first, guess never.

sections.heading: What is actually being tested
sections.body: Fill-in-the-blank questions test grammar (correct tense/preposition/article), vocabulary (correct word for the context/connotation), or both together. A cloze test is a longer passage with MULTIPLE blanks, testing the same skills but requiring you to track the passage's overall meaning and tone across sentences, not just within one isolated sentence.

sections.heading: Strategy for single-sentence fill-in-the-blanks
bullets: Read the WHOLE sentence first, including anything after the blank — the clue is very often placed after the gap, not before it.

Identify what KIND of word is missing: a verb (check tense/agreement), a preposition (check the fixed collocation), a connector (check the logical relationship — contrast, cause, addition), or a content word (check meaning/connotation).
Look for signal words elsewhere in the sentence (already, since, unless, although) that lock in the correct tense or logical connector.
Eliminate options that are grammatically wrong FIRST, then choose the best fit in meaning among what's left.

sections.heading: Strategy for cloze passages
bullets: Read the ENTIRE passage once without trying to fill any blank — this builds the overall context and tone (formal/informal, positive/negative) that individual blanks depend on.
Solve the 'easy' blanks first (ones with an obvious grammar rule or an unambiguous meaning) — these often confirm the passage's tense/tone and make later blanks easier.
Watch for consistency: if the passage has established Past Simple narration, a later blank usually continues in the same tense unless a clear signal word says otherwise.
Re-read the completed passage at the end to check that all your chosen words make it flow logically — an answer that looks fine alone can still break the passage's overall sense.

sections.heading: A special high-yield case: logical connector blanks
sections.body: Many blanks (in cloze tests especially) are actually testing whether you can identify the logical relationship between two clauses/sentences: CONTRAST (however, although, whereas, nevertheless), CAUSE-EFFECT (because, therefore, consequently, as a result), ADDITION (moreover, furthermore, in addition), and CONDITION (if, unless, provided that). Identify the relationship in meaning FIRST, then pick the connector that matches it — this is far more reliable than guessing from the connector's 'feel'.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Fill-in-the-blank and cloze questions test grammar and vocabulary in context — solved by reading the full sentence/passage for clues before evaluating options.
keyFacts: The clue to a blank is often placed AFTER it, not before.
Solve easier blanks first in a cloze passage to lock in tense/tone for the harder ones.
Identify the logical relationship (contrast, cause, addition, condition) before choosing a connector word.

highYieldFacts: Reading the full sentence, especially what follows the blank, resolves most single-blank questions without needing to see the options first.
A cloze passage's established tense/tone almost always continues unless a clear signal word interrupts it.
commonTraps: Filling a blank based only on the words immediately before it and ignoring the rest of the sentence.
Choosing an option that is grammatically fine in isolation but breaks the passage's established tense or tone.
mustRemember: In a cloze passage, always do one full silent read before attempting any blank.
possibleQuestions: Fill in the blank: 'She has been working here ___ 2019.' (since/for)
Choose the correct connector: 'He studied hard; ___, he failed the exam.' (however/therefore)
